## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to plan certificate lifecycle automation in Kubernetes, including cert-manager config, Ingress behavior, rollback, and validation.

## Key Concepts
- cert-manager Certificate and ClusterIssuer
- SecretName update triggers Ingress reload
- Renewal timing, ACME vs CA
- Rollback strategy and observability

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: ingress-tls
  namespace: prod
spec:
  secretName: ingress-tls
  dnsNames:
  - app.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: prod-cluster-issuer
    kind: ClusterIssuer
```

```yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: prod-cluster-issuer
spec:

```

## Why This Is Asked

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical, beginner-friendly ability to diagnose and fix overlapping CronJobs—a common reliability issue in Kubernetes environments. It validates understanding of the controls available to prevent concurrent workloads and ensure predictable maintenance windows.

## Key Concepts
- **CronJob**: A Kubernetes resource that runs Jobs on a recurring schedule.
- **concurrencyPolicy**: Controls whether multiple Job instances can run simultaneously:
  - `Allow` (default): Allows concurrent executions
  - `Forbid`: Prevents concurrent runs; skips a new Job if one is already running
  - `Replace`: Replaces the currently running Job with a new one when a new execution is due
- **startingDeadlineSeconds**: Defines a window of time (in seconds) after the scheduled time during which the CronJob is allowed to start. If a scheduled run is missed (due to cluster issues or a concurrent Job), this setting ensures the Job still runs within the deadline rather than being skipped entirely.

## Why This Is Asked

```bash
# Inspect current webhook configuration
kubectl get MutatingWebhookConfiguration <name> -o yaml

  --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/failurePolicy","value":"Ignore"}]'

kubectl patch MutatingWebhookConfiguration <name> \
  --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/timeoutSeconds","value":30}]'

# Monitor pod creation after fix
kubectl get events -n prod --watch
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests understanding of how NetworkPolicy impacts outbound traffic—a common production pitfall that can cause cascading service failures when egress restrictions are applied without proper allowlisting.

## Key Concepts
- **NetworkPolicy**: A namespace-scoped Kubernetes resource that controls traffic flow into and out of pods using pod selectors
- **Egress rules**: Define allowed outbound destinations using cidrBlocks, namespace selectors, and port specifications
- **Debugging workflow**: Inspect existing policies, test connectivity from within the cluster, and apply targeted policy exceptions

## Code Example
```bash
# List all NetworkPolicies in the cluster
kubectl get netpol -A

# Inspect egress rules for a specific NetworkPolicy
kubectl describe netpol <policy-name> -n <namespace>

# Deploy a debug pod for testing
e kubectl run debug-pod --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never -- /bin/sh

# Test connectivity to billing service from debug pod
kubectl exec -it debug-pod -- wget --spider <billing-service-url>:<port>

# Apply minimal egress NetworkPolicy to allow billing service traffic
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-billing-egress
  namespace: <api-namespace>
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  egress:
  - to:
    - pod: {}
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
EOF
```
